studies.title: Chandra et al. (2008): acute light x temperature; separate CO2 response
studies.design: leaf gas exchange; chamber light/temperature combinations; CO2 tested separately
studies.finding: Photosynthesis and transpiration responded differently to combined heat and light. The abstract does not establish a full temperature x light x CO2 factorial response.
studies.algorithmImplication: Use joint exposure and separate carbon/water channels. No digitized response coefficients or outdoor optimum inferred.

studies.title: Tang et al. (2017): hemp leaf nitrogen x temperature physiology
studies.access: Publisher abstract and indexed results/methods; full PDF unavailable
studies.design: hemp; leaf nitrogen, temperature and biochemical model
studies.finding: Photosynthetic capacity depended on leaf nitrogen and temperature; light-capture efficiency differed between growth environments.
studies.algorithmImplication: Useful model architecture and limits. No coefficient port from inaccessible tables; no fertilizer requirement inferred from weather.

studies.title: Tang et al. (2018): whole-canopy water/nitrogen measurements and modelling
studies.design: Futura 75; canopy chambers, field/container experiments, nitrogen and water supply
studies.finding: Sunlit/shaded canopy modelling coupled photosynthesis, stomatal resistance and available water; canopy structure changed under sustained deficit.
studies.algorithmImplication: Prefer a coupled process model to multiplying independent weather percentages. Measured transpiration was an input to stress calculations; this does not prove weather-only prediction of unknown roots.

studies.title: Sheldon et al. (2021): soil drying and VPD response across hemp cultivars
studies.access: Full university-hosted PDF; Tables 1/2 visually checked
studies.design: separate soil-drying and 32 C VPD trials; field comparison
studies.finding: Table rows contain heterogeneous soil-water breakpoints and both segmented and linear transpiration responses. Trial-to-field transfer was imperfect.
studies.algorithmImplication: Retain cultivar/profile uncertainty; no universal VPD or percent-moisture trigger. Preserve the paper's conflicting abstract/body counts instead of inventing prevalence.

studies.title: Rodriguez-Morrison et al. (2021): leaf and whole-plant light responses
studies.design: CBD-dominant indoor cannabis; light gradient and leaf responses over flowering
studies.finding: Leaf photosynthetic responses varied with local light and developmental time and did not directly predict whole-plant light response.
studies.algorithmImplication: Keep leaf physiology, canopy interception and whole-plant outcomes separate. No universal damaging-light threshold from leaf saturation.

studies.title: Bauerle et al. (2020): leaf age and crown position
studies.design: Cherry Wine; 27 sampled leaves across light treatments/crown positions; ages 1-42 days
studies.finding: Photosynthetic capacity declined with leaf age after full expansion, including in leaves that remained green.
studies.algorithmImplication: Plant age is not leaf age. No age-based canopy multiplier without leaf distribution and transfer validation.

studies.title: Mateva et al. (2024): genotype x water regime x light response
studies.design: three CBD-flower hemp genotypes; water treatments, light-response measurements and recovery
studies.finding: Water-regime/genotype responses differed in gas exchange and photoprotection. Source term 0% FC described the no-irrigation treatment.
studies.algorithmImplication: Water availability changes light response; recovery is a state, not immediate reset. Do not interpret the treatment label as literally measured zero root water.

studies.title: Yuan et al. (2024): salt, drought and mycorrhizal combinations
studies.design: hemp; salt/drought/inoculation; three replicate pots, two plants per pot
studies.finding: Combined stresses and inoculation effects were context-dependent. The treatment table includes selected salt-drought cells, not every possible salt x drought combination.
studies.algorithmImplication: Salinity can constrain water uptake in moist medium. Do not infer EC, colonization, a universal synergy multiplier or an untested full response surface.

studies.title: Pena et al. (2025): genotype and drought physiology
studies.design: two contrasting cannabis clones; 32 plants total; genotype x water treatment
studies.finding: Both diffusional and non-diffusional limitations mattered. Most measured interactions were small; exceptions depended on endpoint. Moisture levels measured on different days were explicitly not directly comparable.
studies.algorithmImplication: Do not force every pair into a synergistic interaction or generalize THC/CBD labels into drought classes. Use same-time controls and endpoint-specific effects.

studies.title: Corredor-Perilla et al. (2025): canopy humidity and plant development
studies.design: one type-III genotype; 10 plants per RH treatment; manually modified chamber ventilation
studies.finding: Sustained high-humidity treatment was associated with altered development and lower biomass. Opening/sealing chambers also changed air exchange; harvest times differed.
studies.algorithmImplication: Supporting association, not an isolated RH coefficient. Independent chamber replication is not clearly established. Assumed leaf-temperature offsets cannot validate leaf VPD.

studies.title: Kim et al. (2025): constant versus fluctuating cold exposure
studies.design: one day-neutral inbred population; two runs; constant/fluctuating temperature treatments
studies.finding: Temperature, maturity and different plant endpoints did not have interchangeable responses. Constant and fluctuating schedules were explicitly compared.
studies.algorithmImplication: Retain day/night sequence, duration and stage. No frost survival threshold, universal base temperature or auto-flowering clock transferred from this trial.

studies.title: Kim et al. (2025): light, RH and temperature in cannabis cuttings
studies.design: two Korean hemp cultivars; six cuttings/treatment; separate light, RH and temperature experiments
studies.finding: Rootless-cutting responses depended on cultivar and environment. Temperature experiment used a different substrate from the RH/light experiments.
studies.algorithmImplication: Rootless/establishing plants need their own scope. These were not a complete joint-factor response experiment; no adult-plant humidity target or adult root-temperature coefficient follows.

studies.title: Pangle, Ali and Jenkins (2025): field hemp physiological capacity
studies.design: Boax and Cherry-Wine; 2019 field season; repeated gas exchange, light and CO2 curves
studies.finding: Published Vcmax/Jmax capacities declined later in the season. Stage, leaf age, nitrogen and season covaried; the site did not impose severe drought.
studies.algorithmImplication: Numerical priors for a tightly scoped research sandbox. Do not identify an independent stage coefficient or reproduce field rates using leaf-temperature assumptions.

studies.title: Holweg et al. (2025): chronic air temperature x light in medical cannabis
studies.access: University primary abstract; full PDF unavailable
studies.design: two genotypes; three light levels; four cultivation cycles with two temperature regimes
studies.finding: Sustained temperature effects depended on genotype and endpoint. Acute leaf-photosynthesis findings did not supply a universal long-term optimum.
studies.algorithmImplication: Strong reason to keep endpoint and duration explicit. No extracted interaction coefficient, inflection temperature or claimed fully crossed randomized temperature design from the abstract.

studies.title: Collado and Hernandez (2025): light history, stage and water use
studies.design: Suver Haze; static/dynamic light histories, greenhouse sunlight, repeated leaf measurements
studies.finding: Instantaneous light and prior light exposure had different effects on transpiration. Whole-crop water use and water use per biomass were distinct endpoints.
studies.algorithmImplication: Track acclimation/history and canopy development. Reported crop-level regression is not a per-pot daily coefficient; water-use efficiency gains do not prove lower absolute plant water use.

S01.title: UC IPM: Broome (1995) and Nair-Allen (1993) Botrytis models
S01.scope: Published grape berry polynomial and grape flower response parameters. Their native tissues and tested domains differ. Both are transferred exposure comparators here. The source fit statistic is not WeedGrow accuracy; their model-disagreement envelope is not a confidence interval.

S02.title: Denton et al. (2025): South African cannabis water use
S02.scope: Full text and PDF reviewed. Field evapotranspiration and stage Kc values support a matching ground-water profile. Field ET includes soil/background evaporation; it cannot be converted into a universal pot dose.

S03.title: Chandra et al. (2011): temperature response of cannabis genotypes
S03.scope: Seven genotypes had different photosynthetic temperature responses; optima spanned approximately 25-35 C. Gas-exchange response is not outdoor air-temperature injury probability. Supports cultivar uncertainty, not the proposed 32 C alert cutoff.

S04.title: Seifi et al. (2025): cannabis powdery mildew resistance
S04.scope: Full methods reviewed: inoculated plants were held at 23 C/80% RH for 48 hours, then 70% RH during continued growth and later scoring. Infection in this protocol contradicts an 85% RH necessary-condition screen; it does not identify a minimum humidity or a complete field response curve.

S05.title: Buirs, Lung and Punja (2025): cannabis bud rot epidemiology
S05.scope: Publisher abstract and indexed methods reviewed; full PDF access unavailable. In a 49-day flowering cycle, inoculation timing affected disease, symptoms appeared later, and measured flower microclimate differed from ambient. Supports exposure history and local drying context; no universal outdoor flower correction or fitted WeedGrow weights.

S06.title: Punja (2026): HLVd and cannabis fungal susceptibility
S06.scope: Publisher abstract/indexed methods reviewed; full PDF access unavailable. Cannabis PM development was reported under 21-25 C and 65% RH, with genotype-dependent effects associated with HLVd status. Do not infer HLVd from weather, apply an unmeasured multiplier, or treat a strain label as a resistance assay.

S07.title: Cannabis germplasm field resistance to G. ambrosiae (2026)
S07.scope: Publisher abstract and indexed discussion reviewed; full PDF access unavailable. New York field seasons show germplasm and phenology differences. Weather associations across two seasons do not identify independent weather coefficients. Supplementary and germplasm records are follow-up data sources, not downloaded training data in this work.

S08.title: Kumar et al. (2026): short-term cannabis waterlogging, Crops 6(5):90
S08.scope: Peer-reviewed 25 September 2026 article, DOI 10.3390/crops6050090. Full public PDF reviewed; Tables 2 and 3 visually checked. Experiment 2 has five replicates/group, Ferimon 12, controlled inundation, early versus flower-initiation treatments and 3/6-day durations. This report fits four rounded group means; individual data were not obtained.

S09.title: Kim et al. (2010): portability of leaf-wetness estimation
S09.scope: Primary full paper reviewed. Weather-based wetness estimation is feasible but site/sensor dependent. Fuzzy-model mean absolute errors at painted-sensor sites ranged 1.1-4.0 hours/day; these are neither a confidence interval nor an error estimate for WeedGrow. The paper's complete fuzzy model is not implemented here.

S10.title: Cornell NEWA: TOMCAST tomato disease model table
S10.scope: Primary extension model documentation, including temperature/wetness DSV lookup. This prototype ports only the lookup as a general wet-leaf exposure comparator. It does not implement the full TOMCAST day, interruption/reset rules, spray program or cannabis pathogen validation.

S11.title: FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56: water balance
S11.scope: Physical basis for root-zone storage, depletion and ET accounting. Application requires supported parameters, units, rooting domain and retained water inputs. Not a justification for fixed watering days from age or pot volume alone.

S12.title: OpenWeather One Call 3.0 API documentation
S12.scope: Provider field definitions, including units, rain intervals and alert structures. Endpoint, entitlement and raw hourly storage must be verified for the actual deployment. A current rain rate, daily forecast amount and precipitation probability are different inputs.

S13.title: Oregon State University: the disease triangle
S13.scope: Disease requires a susceptible host, pathogen and suitable environment. A weather model observes only part of this process; favourable conditions are not a diagnosis.

S14.scope: A useful architecture example coupling weather, host phenology and inoculum. Reported epidemic classification was 17/21 apparent and 15/21 cross-validated, not evidence of 81% cannabis accuracy. Its numerous grape parameters cannot be silently transferred.
